title: Tables, rows, and relationships
summary: Turn the notes app’s saved information into a few small tables, then follow a request to the right rows.
objectives: Read a table as a collection of records with named fields.
Choose an identifier that does not change when a display name changes.
Connect a note to its owner using a relationship.
Read a small SQL query without memorizing the whole language.

terms.definition: A named collection of records organized into columns.
One record in a table, such as one saved note.
A named field shared by the table’s rows, such as title.
A column or combination whose value uniquely identifies each row.
A database rule that a referenced identifier must exist in another specified set of rows.
A language for asking a relational database to read and change data.

retrieval: In the notes app, why does closing the browser not have to delete a saved note?
What information must the server receive to know which note you want?

sections.title: A note needs a predictable place
sections.markdown:
Our small app already saves notes and photos. Maya now has thirty notes, and Arun has twenty. The server needs to answer “show Maya’s notes” without accidentally returning Arun’s. Putting every note into one long text document would make that task awkward. We need records with a predictable structure.

A table is a named collection of records. Each row is one record, and each column is one kind of fact. Imagine a carefully labeled spreadsheet: one row per note, columns for the note’s identifier, owner, title, and text.

A database adds rules and query operations that an ordinary shared spreadsheet may not provide in the same way. It can reject duplicate identifiers and preserve related changes, which we will explore next week. The analogy helps you picture rows; it is not a claim that every spreadsheet behavior matches a database.

Start with two tables, users and notes. Separate them because one user can own several notes. Maya’s name belongs in one user row rather than being copied into every note. A later name change should not require finding and editing all thirty copies.

sections.title: Give each thing a stable identifier
sections.markdown:
Here is our small example. The numbers are chosen for the exercise, not generated by a special algorithm.

| user_id | display_name |
|---:|---|
| 7 | Maya |
| 9 | Arun |

| note_id | owner_id | title |
|---:|---:|---|
| 41 | 7 | Garden photo |
| 42 | 7 | Weekend plan |
| 43 | 9 | Reading list |

Keep three roles separate:

| Value | Role | What can change without changing the note? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| note_id = 42 | **Primary key:** identifies one note row | Keep this stable |
| owner_id = 7 | Relationship to a user identity | Ownership changes require an explicit rule |
| title = Weekend plan | Editable display text | Rename it or reuse the same title on another note |

The users table similarly uses user_id as its primary key. Display names and titles make poor identities because people expect to edit them and duplicates are possible.

The owner_id column creates a relationship: note 41 belongs to user 7. A foreign-key rule can reject a new note whose owner_id is 99 when no such user exists. It does not decide whether the caller is allowed to act as user 7. That permission check remains part of the application’s behavior. A well-connected row can still be exposed to the wrong person if the server forgets access control.

sections.title: Read a query one clause at a time
sections.markdown:
SQL lets us ask for selected columns from matching rows. This request asks for Maya’s notes in identifier order:

~~~sql
SELECT note_id, title
FROM notes
WHERE owner_id = 7
ORDER BY note_id;
~~~

Read the query as a question about the answer: from notes, keep owner 7, return the identity and title, and order by identity. The visible result is:

| note_id | title |
| --- | --- |
| 41 | Garden photo |
| 42 | Weekend plan |

Row 43 belongs to owner 9, so it does not pass this condition. SELECT describes the answer; it does not itself mean “fast.” The index chapter explains how the database can reduce search work.

The example shows a literal 7 so the condition is easy to see. In real application code, the server obtains the authenticated user’s identifier from its trusted login handling and passes it as a query parameter. A parameter is a separate value supplied to the database driver, rather than text pasted into SQL. Do not turn user-entered text into query instructions by string concatenation. You need not implement a driver today; remember that values and query structure are different.

When a page needs the owner’s display name, a join can match notes.owner_id to users.user_id and combine those related facts in the result. A join is a matching operation, not a command to merge the stored tables permanently. For our three rows, both notes 41 and 42 match Maya’s one user row.

sections.title: Store only what the current question needs
sections.markdown:
The table layout is called a schema: the named fields, their kinds of values, and their rules. An integer field holds a whole number; a text field holds characters. A required title rule can reject a missing title. A maximum allowed title length can prevent unexpectedly huge inputs. Choose rules from the product’s needs, rather than adding columns because another app has them.

For a photo note, we can keep the title and owner in notes and a reference to a separate stored photo. The photo’s bytes are the image content; a reference tells us where to retrieve it. Later we will compare storage choices. Today the important point is that a record can describe a file without putting the entire image into every list response.

Walk the complete read path: Maya requests her list, the server establishes her user identifier, the query selects matching rows, and the server returns the permitted fields. The browser displays titles. Nothing in this path requires knowing every SQL keyword or choosing several database products.

Your stopping point is practical: draw the two tiny tables, point to their primary keys, and follow note 41 to its owner. Then change Maya’s display name. Only her user row needs that change; the note-owner relationship still uses 7. That is the benefit of separating identity, display text, and relationships.

> **Interview phrasing:** “I would keep the user’s current name in one user row and store the owner identity on each note. That lets a rename update one fact while queries still follow the relationship.”

flowchart LR
U[User 7: Maya] -->|owns| N1[Note 41: Garden photo]

A[User 9: Arun] -->|owns| N3[Note 43: Reading list]
diagrams.caption: The arrows mean ownership relationships, not network messages. Each note row stores its owner’s identifier.
steps: Locate user 7 once in the users table.
Rename Maya without changing either note identifier or owner identifier.

diagrams.title: A query selects both rows and columns
diagrams.source:
flowchart LR
T[Notes 41 and 42 and 43] --> F[Keep owner 7]
F --> R[Matching notes 41 and 42]
R --> C[Return note ID and title]
C --> O[Order by note ID]
diagrams.caption: This is reasoning about the requested result, not a promise about physical execution order. Permission scope must be supplied correctly by the application.
steps: Choose the table containing the facts.
Apply the owner condition to decide which rows qualify.
Choose the returned columns and an explicit order.

exercise.prompt: Add note 44, titled Weekend plan, for Arun. List its owner_id, explain why its title may match note 42, and predict the query result for owner_id=9.
rubric: Returns notes 43 and 44 for Arun, not 42.
exercise.solution: The new row is (note_id = 44, owner_id = 9, title = Weekend plan). Titles are editable labels and may repeat; note_id is the unique identity. The query for owner 9 returns 43/Reading list and 44/Weekend plan. The identical title does not transfer ownership or combine the records.

questions.explanation: Titles and names can change or repeat.

questions.prompt: A foreign key proves the requesting browser owns a note:
questions.explanation: It checks a stored relationship, while the server still checks permission.

questions.prompt: Why put a user’s display name in a users table instead of every note?
questions.answer: One user can own many notes, so storing the name once avoids many copies that could disagree after a rename.
questions.explanation: Use the owner identifier to connect notes to that one record.

questions.prompt: Describe what a join does in this example.
questions.answer: It matches notes.owner_id with users.user_id so a query result can include the owner’s display name alongside a note.
questions.explanation: It combines related facts in a result without permanently combining the two tables.

flashcards.back: One record, such as one note.
A unique identifier for a row.
A rule that a referenced identifier exists in the specified table/key.
Selects which rows match the requested condition.

flashcards.front: Why keep identity separate from title?
flashcards.back: Titles may repeat or change while the record remains the same.

mentalModel: A table gives each fact a predictable place; keys connect the facts without depending on editable names.

walkthroughs.title: A rename changes one fact while relationships remain
walkthroughs.intro: Use the tiny tables above. We are changing a display name, not the identity or ownership of any note.

steps.title: Read the current records
steps.explanation: Both notes refer to user 7. They do not need their own permanent copy of the user’s current name.

steps.title: Rename the user
steps.explanation: The application changes the name on the user row under its normal validation and permission rules.

steps.title: Join for a display
steps.explanation: A query matches owner_id 7 to user_id 7 and obtains the current name.

walkthroughs.takeaway: A relationship points to a stable identity. The display text can change without rewriting every referring record.
